questions.subject: bio
questions.q: How many daughter cells are produced when one body cell divides by mitosis?
questions.hint: Think of one cell splitting into copies of itself.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which statement best describes the cells produced by mitosis?
options: They are genetically identical to the parent cell
They have half the number of chromosomes
questions.answer: They are genetically identical to the parent cell
questions.hint: Mitosis is used for growth and repair, so the new cells must match the old ones.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Name the type of cell division that produces gametes.
questions.hint: It takes place in the testes and ovaries.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A human body cell contains 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are found in a human sperm cell?
questions.hint: Gametes contain one set of chromosomes, not two.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which of these is NOT a role of mitosis?
questions.hint: Which process needs cells with half the usual number of chromosomes?

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What happens to the DNA in a cell before it divides by mitosis?
questions.hint: Each new cell needs a full set of chromosomes.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Meiosis is described as a ___ division because the chromosome number is halved. Write the missing word.
questions.hint: The number of chromosomes goes down.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: How many gametes are produced from one cell that divides by meiosis?
questions.hint: Meiosis involves two divisions in a row.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Why does meiosis produce genetic variation?
options: Each gamete receives a different combination of chromosomes
Each gamete is a copy of the parent cell
Gametes have twice as many chromosomes
questions.answer: Each gamete receives a different combination of chromosomes
questions.hint: Think about how chromosomes are shared out between the new cells.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Where are adult stem cells found in humans?
questions.hint: This tissue makes new blood cells throughout life.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: In plants, where are stem cells found?
questions.hint: Look for the regions of a plant that keep growing, such as root and shoot tips.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What is the name of the process by which a stem cell becomes a specialised cell?
questions.hint: The cell becomes different from the original unspecialised cell.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What is the main advantage of embryonic stem cells compared with adult stem cells?
options: They can differentiate into almost any type of cell
They are always easy to obtain
questions.answer: They can differentiate into almost any type of cell
questions.hint: Adult stem cells can only form a limited range of cells.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A cell divides by mitosis once every 24 hours, and every new cell also divides. Starting with one cell, how many cells will there be after 3 days?
questions.hint: The number of cells doubles each time.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Explain why gametes must be produced by meiosis rather than mitosis for sexual reproduction to work.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the chromosome number at fertilisation.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Evaluate the use of embryonic stem cells to treat diseases.
questions.hint: Give benefits and concerns (ethical and medical), then reach a judgement.

bss.topic: Climas do Brasil e massas de ar

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual tipo climático predomina na Amazônia?
questions.hint: Pense na região perto da linha do Equador, quente e muito chuvosa.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual característica é típica do clima semiárido do Nordeste?
questions.hint: É o clima do Sertão, com longos períodos de seca.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Em qual região do Brasil predomina o clima subtropical?
questions.hint: É a região mais distante da linha do Equador.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual massa de ar quente e úmida se forma sobre a Amazônia?
questions.hint: Ela se forma sobre o continente, numa área de floresta e muita umidade.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Quais são as características da massa Polar atlântica (mPa)?
options: Fria e seca, vinda do Pacífico
questions.hint: Ela se forma sobre o oceano, no sul do continente.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como se chama a queda brusca de temperatura que às vezes ocorre na Amazônia quando a massa Polar atlântica avança até lá?
questions.hint: O nome vem da sensação de frio repentino.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Em um climograma, o que geralmente representam as barras verticais?
options: A umidade do ar em cada hora
questions.hint: A linha costuma representar outra variável.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual é a característica principal do clima tropical típico do Brasil Central?
options: Chuva bem distribuída o ano todo
questions.hint: Pense nas duas estações bem marcadas do Cerrado.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Por que o clima tropical de altitude tem temperaturas mais amenas que o tropical típico?
options: Porque ocorre em áreas mais elevadas
Porque fica mais perto do Equador
Porque recebe a massa Equatorial continental
questions.answer: Porque ocorre em áreas mais elevadas
questions.hint: A temperatura diminui conforme se sobe.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual massa de ar, quente e úmida, se forma sobre o oceano Atlântico e atua no litoral leste do Brasil?
questions.hint: Ela se forma na zona tropical, sobre o mar.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual é a característica da massa Tropical continental (mTc)?
questions.hint: Ela se forma sobre uma área continental no interior da América do Sul, longe do mar.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como se chama a chuva provocada pelo encontro de uma massa de ar fria com uma massa de ar quente?
questions.hint: O nome vem da 'frente' que se forma entre as duas massas.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Por que a temperatura média anual de Porto Alegre é menor que a de Manaus?
options: Porque Porto Alegre está em maior latitude
Porque Porto Alegre está mais perto do Equador
Porque Manaus recebe a massa Polar atlântica com mais frequência
questions.answer: Porque Porto Alegre está em maior latitude
questions.hint: Compare a distância de cada cidade até a linha do Equador.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Um climograma mostra temperaturas entre 25 °C e 28 °C o ano inteiro e mais de 2.000 mm de chuva por ano. Que clima ele representa?
questions.hint: Calor constante e muita chuva.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Explique como a atuação da massa Polar atlântica influencia o inverno nas regiões Sul e Sudeste.
questions.hint: Pense em temperatura, frentes frias e geadas.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Explique por que as chuvas no Sertão nordestino são escassas e irregulares.
questions.hint: Considere como as massas de ar chegam à região e o papel do relevo.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which formula is used to calculate the gross profit margin?
questions.hint: A margin compares a profit figure with sales.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A business has revenue of $200,000 and gross profit of $80,000. Calculate its gross profit margin (%).
questions.hint: Divide gross profit by revenue, then multiply by 100.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A business has revenue of $500,000 and profit of $50,000. Calculate its profit margin (%).
questions.hint: Profit ÷ revenue × 100.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A business makes a profit of $60,000 and has capital employed of $400,000. Calculate its ROCE (%).
questions.hint: Profit ÷ capital employed × 100.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: What does return on capital employed (ROCE) measure?
options: How efficiently a business uses its capital to generate profit
How quickly a business can pay its short-term debts
How much stock a business holds
How many customers a business has
questions.answer: How efficiently a business uses its capital to generate profit
questions.hint: Think about the money invested in the business.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Gross profit = revenue minus ___. Write the missing term.
questions.hint: These are the direct costs of the products sold.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which change is most likely to increase a business's gross profit margin?
options: Finding a cheaper supplier of materials
Paying higher wages to office staff
questions.answer: Finding a cheaper supplier of materials
questions.hint: Gross profit is affected only by revenue and direct costs.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A firm's gross profit margin stays the same, but its profit margin falls. What is the most likely reason?
options: Its cost of sales has fallen
questions.hint: What is subtracted between gross profit and profit?

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A shop has revenue of $80,000 and cost of sales of $50,000. Calculate its gross profit margin (%).
questions.hint: First work out gross profit.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A business has a gross profit margin of 25% and revenue of $120,000. Calculate its gross profit in dollars.
questions.hint: 25% of revenue.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which stakeholder group is most likely to use ROCE when deciding whether to invest in a company?
questions.hint: Who wants a return on the money they put in?

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Why should a business compare its profitability ratios with previous years or with competitors?
options: A single ratio means little on its own
It makes the ratios more accurate
It is required for every sale
questions.answer: A single ratio means little on its own
questions.hint: Is 12% good or bad? It depends on what you compare it with.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Using ratios to assess a business's performance is called ___ analysis. Write the missing word.
questions.hint: The word is in the name of the figures being used.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A business has a ROCE of 12% and capital employed of $250,000. Calculate its profit in dollars.
questions.hint: Rearrange the ROCE formula.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Explain one limitation of using profitability ratios to judge a business's performance.
questions.hint: Think about what the figures do not show, or how old they are.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A company's ROCE fell from 14% last year to 8% this year. Analyse two possible reasons for this fall.
questions.hint: Consider changes in profit and changes in capital employed.

chem.topic: Alcohols: manufacture of ethanol and its uses

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which raw material is used to make ethanol by fermentation?
questions.hint: Fermentation uses a renewable resource.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Name the microorganism used to ferment sugar into ethanol.
questions.hint: It is also used to make bread rise.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which conditions are used for fermentation?
options: Room temperature with plenty of oxygen
questions.hint: Living cells carry out this reaction, and it is anaerobic.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Why is fermentation not carried out at a high temperature such as 80 °C?
options: The enzymes in yeast would be denatured
The sugar would turn into ethene
The reaction would need more oxygen
questions.answer: The enzymes in yeast would be denatured
questions.hint: Yeast relies on proteins that are damaged by heat.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What are the products of the fermentation of glucose?
questions.hint: One product is a gas that makes bubbles.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Glucose ferments: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. How many moles of ethanol are produced from 1 mole of glucose?
questions.hint: Read the number in front of ethanol in the equation.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which catalyst is used in the hydration of ethene to make ethanol?
questions.hint: It is an acid catalyst.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which conditions are used for the catalytic addition of steam to ethene?
questions.hint: It needs a high temperature and a high pressure.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: The ethene used to make ethanol is obtained by ___ long-chain alkanes from crude oil. Write the missing word.
questions.hint: This process breaks large molecules into smaller ones.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What is one advantage of making ethanol by fermentation?
options: It uses a renewable raw material
It is a fast, continuous process
questions.answer: It uses a renewable raw material
questions.hint: Where does the sugar come from?

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What is one advantage of making ethanol by hydration of ethene?
options: It is fast and produces pure ethanol
It uses a renewable raw material
questions.answer: It is fast and produces pure ethanol
questions.hint: Compare the speed and purity of the two methods.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which separation method is used to obtain concentrated ethanol from the fermentation mixture?
questions.hint: It separates liquids with different boiling points.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of ethanol, C₂H₅OH. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.hint: Count every atom: 2 C, 6 H and 1 O.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Balance the equation for the complete combustion of ethanol: C₂H₅OH + __O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. What number goes in the gap?
questions.hint: Count the oxygen atoms on the right, then subtract the one already in ethanol.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Ethanol made by fermentation can be called a biofuel. Why?
options: It is made from plant material
It does not produce carbon dioxide when burned
questions.answer: It is made from plant material
questions.hint: 'Bio' refers to living things.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Compare the manufacture of ethanol by fermentation and by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene.
questions.hint: Consider raw materials, conditions, rate, purity and whether the process is batch or continuous.

comp.topic: Databases: single-table databases, fields, records and primary keys

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In a single-table database, what is a record?
options: A complete set of data about one item, shown as a row
A single category of data, shown as a column
questions.answer: A complete set of data about one item, shown as a row
questions.hint: Think of one line of data about one thing.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In a single-table database, what is a field?
options: One category of data, shown as a column
A complete row of data about one item
questions.answer: One category of data, shown as a column
questions.hint: Think of a heading such as 'Surname'.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: State the name given to the field that uniquely identifies each record in a table.
questions.hint: It is the 'key' that tells records apart.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which data type is most suitable for storing a person's date of birth?
questions.hint: The value is a day, month and year.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A field called HasPaidFee can only be Yes or No. Which data type is most suitable?
questions.hint: Only two possible values.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which data type should be used for a telephone number such as 01632 960123?
questions.hint: Think about the leading zero and the space.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which field would make the best primary key in a table of library books?
questions.hint: Which value could never be shared by two books?

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A table holds data about 250 cars, with 8 fields for each car. How many records are in the table?
questions.hint: One record per car.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A table holds data about 250 cars, with 8 fields for each car. How many individual data items does the table store?
questions.hint: Records × fields.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which data type is most suitable for a Price field storing values such as 12.99?
questions.hint: The value has a decimal part.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which data type is most suitable for a NumberOfPages field?
questions.hint: Pages are counted in whole numbers.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A field stores a single grade letter such as A, B or C. Which data type is most suitable?
questions.hint: It is one letter only.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which statement about a primary key is true?
options: It must contain a unique value for every record
It must always be a text field
It can be left blank for some records
Every table needs at least two
questions.answer: It must contain a unique value for every record
questions.hint: Think about what 'identifies' means.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Explain why Surname would not be a suitable primary key in a table of students.
questions.hint: Could two students share the same value?

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A vet stores data about pets in one table. Suggest a suitable primary key and explain your choice.
questions.hint: Think of a value created to be different for every pet.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Identify two fields, each with a suitable data type, for a table storing details of films shown at a cinema.
questions.hint: Think of text, number and date values about a film.

econ.topic: Applied microeconomics: demand and supply diagrams in current events

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A frost destroys much of the coffee harvest. Which change happens in the coffee market?
questions.hint: Less coffee can be produced at every price.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: After the frost, what happens to the equilibrium price and quantity of coffee?
questions.hint: Follow the new curve to the new equilibrium.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A popular online star promotes a brand of trainers. What happens in the market for those trainers?
questions.hint: Tastes and preferences have changed.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: The government introduces an indirect tax on sugary drinks. What happens to the supply curve?
questions.hint: The tax raises producers' costs.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Incomes fall during a recession. What happens to demand for a normal good?
questions.hint: Normal goods are bought more when incomes rise.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: The price of petrol rises sharply. What is the likely effect on demand for large petrol cars?
questions.hint: Petrol and cars are used together.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What term describes the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied?
questions.hint: The market is 'balanced' here.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: New technology cuts the cost of making solar panels. What happens to equilibrium?
questions.hint: Lower costs shift supply to the right.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: If a price is set above the equilibrium price, what results?
questions.hint: Compare quantity supplied with quantity demanded.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A heatwave raises demand for ice cream while higher milk prices raise costs. What can be said for certain?
questions.hint: Both shifts push one variable the same way.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: On a demand and supply diagram, what is shown on the vertical axis?
questions.hint: The horizontal axis shows quantity.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: The government gives a subsidy to wheat farmers. What happens to the supply of wheat?
questions.hint: A subsidy lowers producers' costs.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Concert tickets are resold for far more than their original price. What does this suggest?
options: Excess demand at the original price
Excess supply at the original price
questions.answer: Excess demand at the original price
questions.hint: More people wanted tickets than were available.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Using a demand and supply diagram, explain the effect of a new tax on cigarettes on the market for cigarettes.
questions.hint: Which curve shifts? Describe the new price and quantity.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A news report says avocado prices have risen as avocados became more popular. Explain why the price has risen, using demand and supply.
questions.hint: Think about a change in tastes.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A drought reduces the wheat harvest. Explain how this could affect the market for bread.
questions.hint: Wheat is a raw material for bread.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: In a 45-minute narrative composition, roughly how long should you spend planning?
questions.hint: Enough to plan, but leave most time for writing.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which is a common simple plan for a short story?
questions.hint: Think of the shape of a story.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which opening is most likely to engage the reader?
options: The door had been locked for eleven years, until tonight.
This is a story about a door.
Once upon a time there was a door.
I am going to tell you about a door.
questions.answer: The door had been locked for eleven years, until tonight.
questions.hint: Which one makes you ask a question?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What does 'show, don't tell' mean?
options: Reveal feelings through actions, dialogue and detail
questions.answer: Reveal feelings through actions, dialogue and detail
questions.hint: Let the reader work out the feeling.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the term for a narrative told by a character using 'I'?
questions.hint: Count the pronoun: I, you, or he/she.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the best way to manage a 350–450 word story?
options: Focus on one key event over a short time
Add as many plot twists as possible
questions.answer: Focus on one key event over a short time
questions.hint: The word limit is tight.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which technique is used in 'Footsteps. Closer. Then nothing.'?
questions.hint: Look at the length of each sentence.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What term describes a scene that moves back to an earlier time in the story?
questions.hint: It looks back in time.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which ending is generally most effective in a timed story?
options: One that links back to the opening
'And then I woke up – it was all a dream.'
Stopping mid-sentence when time runs out
Introducing a new character in the last line
questions.answer: One that links back to the opening
questions.hint: A circular structure feels complete.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Why should you leave about 5 minutes at the end?
options: To check spelling, punctuation and paragraphing
questions.answer: To check spelling, punctuation and paragraphing
questions.hint: Accuracy is also marked.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What punctuation marks go around the words a character speaks?
questions.hint: They open and close the dialogue.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which sentence best appeals to the senses?
options: The smell of burnt toast drifted under the door.
questions.answer: The smell of burnt toast drifted under the door.
questions.hint: Which one could you smell, hear or see?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: When should you start a new paragraph in a narrative?
options: When the time, place, speaker or topic changes
questions.answer: When the time, place, speaker or topic changes
questions.hint: Remember TiPToP.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Write an opening sentence for a story called 'The Last Train' that creates mystery.
questions.hint: Hold back some information.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Explain two ways a writer can build tension near the climax of a story.
questions.hint: Think about sentence length, pace and detail.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: In note form, give a setting, a main character and the central problem for a story called 'The Storm'.
questions.hint: Keep each note short and specific.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: In a 45-minute unseen poetry answer, what should you do first?
options: Read the poem and the question carefully, at least twice
Count the syllables in every line
questions.answer: Read the poem and the question carefully, at least twice
questions.hint: Understanding comes before analysis.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What term describes the voice speaking in a poem?
questions.hint: It is not always the poet.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is enjambment?
options: When a sentence runs over a line break without punctuation
A pause in the middle of a line
questions.answer: When a sentence runs over a line break without punctuation
questions.hint: Look at the ends of lines.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: 'The city is a sleeping beast' is an example of which device?
questions.hint: There is no 'like' or 'as'.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: A poem uses words such as 'grey', 'hollow' and 'cold'. Which word best describes its tone?
questions.hint: What mood do these words share?

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is a pause in the middle of a line of poetry called?
questions.hint: It is often marked by a full stop or comma mid-line.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What does a strong analytical paragraph usually include?
options: A point, a short quotation and analysis of its effect
questions.answer: A point, a short quotation and analysis of its effect
questions.hint: Think PEA or PEE.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: 'Whispering waves wandered' is an example of which device?
questions.hint: Listen to the first sounds.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: A poem with no regular rhyme or metre is written in…
questions.hint: It is 'free' of fixed patterns.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What term describes a group of lines in a poem?
questions.hint: It is like a paragraph in poetry.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Why should you comment on a poem's structure?
options: Because form and structure help create meaning
To show you can count lines
questions.answer: Because form and structure help create meaning
questions.hint: How does the shape support the ideas?

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which phrase is the most precise way to begin analysis?
options: The image evokes a sense of loss
questions.answer: The image evokes a sense of loss
questions.hint: Choose a verb that explains an effect.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: In the line 'The clock, the clock, the clock kept on', what does the repetition mainly do?
options: Emphasises the slow, relentless passing of time
questions.answer: Emphasises the slow, relentless passing of time
questions.hint: Think about the rhythm of a ticking clock.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Why is it useful to explore more than one interpretation in an unseen poetry answer?
questions.hint: Think about what examiners reward.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Read: 'My grandmother's hands were maps / of every field she'd ever worked.' Explore the effect of the metaphor.
questions.hint: What might the lines on a map suggest?

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Explain how you would plan and structure a 45-minute response to an unseen poem.
questions.hint: Think about timing, paragraphs and an overview.

fmath.topic: Integrating eˣ, 1/(ax + b) and trigonometric functions

questions.subject: fmath
questions.q: Find ∫ e^(3x) dx.
questions.hint: Divide by the coefficient of x.

questions.subject: fmath
questions.q: Find ∫ (2x + 1)⁴ dx.
questions.hint: Raise the power by one, then divide by the new power and by 2.

questions.subject: fmath
questions.q: Find ∫ 1/(4x + 3) dx.
questions.hint: The integral of 1/u is ln|u|; remember the 4.

questions.subject: fmath
questions.q: Find ∫ cos(2x) dx.
questions.hint: Integrating cos gives sin; divide by 2.

questions.subject: fmath
questions.q: Find ∫ sin(3x) dx.
questions.hint: Integrating sin gives minus cos.

questions.subject: fmath
questions.q: Find ∫ e^(2x + 1) dx.
questions.hint: Differentiate each option to check.

questions.subject: fmath
questions.q: Find ∫ 6/(2x − 1) dx.

questions.subject: fmath
questions.q: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 1 of e^(2x) dx, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π/2 of cos x dx.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π/6 of sin(2x) dx, giving an exact fraction.

questions.q: Find the exact value of ∫ from 1 to 3 of 1/x dx.

questions.subject: fmath
questions.q: Find ∫ (3x − 2)⁻² dx.

questions.subject: fmath
questions.q: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 1 of (2x + 1)³ dx.

questions.subject: fmath
questions.q: Find ∫ (4e^(2x) − cos x) dx.
questions.hint: Integrate each term separately.

books.title: Luz e Sombra no Pátio
books.premise: Três amigos do primeiro ano preparam um sarau barroco e cada um estuda uma vertente do poeta baiano apelidado de Boca do Inferno: a lírica, a religiosa e a satírica. Entre antíteses, argumentos e uma sátira que mira o alvo errado, eles descobrem o conflito que une as três faces do poeta.

chapters.title: Capítulo 1: Três faces de um poeta
chapters.synopsis: A professora Celeste apresenta o poeta baiano do Barroco e propõe um sarau. Lia, Tomás e Rafa sorteiam qual vertente cada um vai estudar.
chapters.text:
Na segunda-feira, a professora Celeste entrou na sala do primeiro ano carregando uma caixa de papelão velha e um sorriso de quem prepara uma armadilha. Escreveu na lousa, em letras grandes: "Luz e sombra. Pecado e perdão. Riso e veneno."
— Essas três duplas resumem o poeta que vamos estudar — disse ela. — Um baiano do século XVII, que viveu entre Salvador e Portugal e ganhou um apelido nada simpático: Boca do Inferno.
A turma riu. Rafa, que sentava no fundo, levantou a cabeça pela primeira vez na manhã.
A professora explicou que o Barroco nasceu de um tempo dividido. De um lado, a Contrarreforma lembrava as pessoas do pecado, da morte e da salvação da alma. De outro, o mundo oferecia prazeres, riquezas e beleza. O artista barroco vivia preso entre esses dois polos, e por isso a sua linguagem era cheia de antíteses, paradoxos e jogos de palavras.
— O nosso poeta escreveu em três direções — continuou. — Há a poesia lírica, que fala do amor e da passagem do tempo; a poesia religiosa, em que o eu lírico conversa com Deus, arrependido; e a poesia satírica, que zomba dos vícios da Bahia colonial. Três faces, um mesmo homem.
Então ela abriu a caixa. Dentro havia três papéis dobrados.
— Daqui a seis semanas faremos um sarau barroco no pátio. Cada grupo vai estudar uma vertente e escrever um poema original no estilo dela. Nada de copiar: quero ver vocês pensando como barrocos.
Lia, Tomás e Rafa formavam um trio desde o fundamental. Lia era a que anotava tudo com canetas coloridas; Tomás, o que fazia perguntas que ninguém esperava; Rafa, o que fazia piadas na hora errada. Cada um puxou um papel.
Lia abriu o dela e leu em voz alta:
— Lírica.
Tomás olhou o seu e franziu a testa:
— Religiosa. Logo eu, que só vou à missa no Natal.
Rafa desdobrou o último devagar, como quem abre um bilhete premiado, e soltou uma gargalhada.
— Satírica! Professora, a senhora sorteou certo.
— Cuidado — respondeu Celeste, sem tirar o sorriso. — A sátira é a vertente mais divertida e também a mais perigosa. O poeta pagou caro por ela.
Na saída, os três se sentaram na escada da biblioteca. Lia desenhou um triângulo no caderno e escreveu uma vertente em cada ponta.
— Se é o mesmo poeta, deve haver alguma coisa que liga as três — disse ela.
— O conflito — arriscou Tomás. — A professora falou que o barroco vive dividido.
Rafa já rabiscava rimas no braço da cadeira.
— Eu só sei que vou ser o Boca do Inferno da escola.
Lia fechou o caderno e encarou o amigo.
— Então começa estudando, Boca. Sexta-feira cada um traz a primeira versão.
Rafa bateu continência, e os três desceram a escada rindo, sem imaginar quanto aquela brincadeira ainda ia render.

chapters.title: Capítulo 2: O relógio de Lia
chapters.synopsis: Lia tenta escrever um poema lírico e descobre o tema da fugacidade do tempo. Com a avó, entende o carpe diem barroco e o cultismo.
chapters.text:
Lia passou três noites olhando para uma página em branco. Sabia tudo o que a apostila dizia sobre a lírica barroca: o amor como conflito, a beleza que se desfaz, o convite para aproveitar a juventude antes que o tempo a leve. Mas, quando tentava escrever, saía um poema de cartão de aniversário.
No sábado, foi visitar a avó Nair, que morava num apartamento cheio de plantas e de relógios antigos. Enquanto a avó regava uma orquídea, Lia reclamou do poema.
— Escreve sobre o quê? — perguntou a avó.
— Sobre o tempo que passa e leva a beleza. Só que fica tudo muito óbvio.
A avó apontou para a orquídea. Na véspera, a flor estava perfeita; agora uma pétala começava a escurecer nas bordas.
— Óbvio é dizer que a flor murcha. Barroco é sofrer porque ela murcha enquanto você ainda está olhando para ela.
Lia ficou parada. Lembrou da aula: a professora Celeste tinha falado que os poetas barrocos comparavam a beleza da moça à flor, ao sol, à luz, e logo depois mostravam a noite, a sombra, a cinza. A antítese não era enfeite; era o próprio drama.
Ela abriu o caderno e escreveu: "Na tua face a rosa amanhece / e já, na mesma face, anoitece". Gostou do som. Depois acrescentou: "goza o jardim enquanto é jardim, / que o tempo é jardineiro sem fim".
— Isso é o carpe diem — disse a avó, lendo por cima do ombro. — Aproveite o dia.
— Mas no Barroco é um carpe diem triste — respondeu Lia, animada. — Não é só "aproveite". É "aproveite porque tudo vai acabar".
Nos dias seguintes, Lia caprichou nas imagens. Encheu o poema de cores, de metáforas preciosas, de inversões na ordem das palavras. Na sexta-feira, leu a versão para os amigos.
Tomás coçou a cabeça.
— É bonito, mas eu me perdi lá pela quarta linha.
A professora Celeste, que passava pelo corredor, pediu para ler. Sorriu.
— Você descobriu o cultismo, Lia: o jogo de palavras, as imagens rebuscadas, a ordem invertida. É muito barroco. Mas o cultismo em excesso esconde a ideia. Tente equilibrar: mantenha a antítese entre o dia e a noite, e corte alguns enfeites.
Lia passou o fim de semana cortando. Cada palavra retirada doía um pouco, como a pétala escura da orquídea. No domingo, o poema tinha dois versos a menos e uma força que antes não tinha.
Ela mandou uma foto do caderno para a avó. A resposta chegou em um minuto: uma foto da orquídea, já sem a pétala, e a legenda "o jardineiro passou por aqui".

chapters.title: Capítulo 3: A discussão de Tomás
chapters.synopsis: Tomás não sabe como escrever um poema religioso até perceber que o eu lírico barroco argumenta com Deus. Ele descobre o conceptismo.
chapters.text:
Tomás tinha um problema sério: achava que poesia religiosa era uma oração rimada, e orações rimadas lhe davam sono. Na biblioteca, folheava a apostila com cara de quem lê bula de remédio.
— Escuta isso — disse Lia, sentando-se ao lado dele. — A professora falou que, nos sonetos religiosos, o eu lírico não só pede perdão. Ele discute com Deus.
Tomás levantou a sobrancelha.
— Discute como?
— Ele argumenta. Diz que pecou muito, sim, mas que isso dá a Deus uma chance maior de mostrar misericórdia. Quanto maior o pecado, maior a glória do perdão.
Tomás largou a apostila.
— Isso é quase um advogado tentando ganhar a causa.
Na aula seguinte, ele levou a ideia para a professora Celeste. Ela confirmou, animada.
— É o conceptismo, Tomás. Enquanto o cultismo brinca com as palavras e as imagens, o conceptismo brinca com as ideias: raciocínios engenhosos, comparações lógicas, paradoxos. O pecador barroco vive o conflito entre a culpa e a esperança, e usa a inteligência para se aproximar do perdão.
— Então o poema pode ter um argumento — disse Tomás, mais para si mesmo do que para ela.
— Deve ter.
Naquela noite, ele pensou num caso concreto. Lembrou da ovelha perdida da parábola que ouvira na infância: o pastor deixa as outras e vai buscar a que se desgarrou. Se a ovelha fosse esperta, pensou, diria ao pastor: "Se você não me buscar, perde uma ovelha e a fama de bom pastor".
Riu sozinho no quarto. Era isso. Escreveu o primeiro quarteto: o eu lírico confessa que se afastou do rebanho. No segundo, admite a culpa sem desculpas. Nos tercetos, vira o jogo: lembra ao pastor que a alegria de encontrar a ovelha perdida é maior do que a de contar as que ficaram.
Quando terminou, contou as sílabas nos dedos, como a professora ensinara, e ajustou dois versos que estavam compridos demais.
Na sexta, leu para o trio. Rafa ficou em silêncio, coisa rara.
— Cara, você fez Deus perder um debate.
— Não — corrigiu Tomás. — O eu lírico não vence. Ele se humilha e, ao mesmo tempo, argumenta. É as duas coisas juntas. Isso é o barroco: o pecador está no chão, mas a cabeça não para de pensar.
Lia anotou a frase com a caneta roxa, a das ideias importantes.
Tomás guardou o poema na mochila com um cuidado que ninguém tinha visto nele antes. Talvez a poesia religiosa não desse tanto sono assim.

chapters.title: Capítulo 4: A cantina de Rafa
chapters.synopsis: Rafa escreve uma sátira sobre a cantina da escola e faz a turma rir. A professora explica que a sátira barroca mirava a sociedade da Bahia colonial.
chapters.text:
Rafa não teve dificuldade nenhuma para começar. Em uma tarde escreveu uma sátira inteira sobre a cantina da escola: o pão de queijo que já nascia frio, o suco "natural" que vinha de pacote, o preço que subia mais rápido do que a nota de matemática dele. Tinha rimas engraçadas, trocadilhos e um refrão que a turma decorou em um dia.
No intervalo, alguém leu o poema em voz alta perto da fila do lanche. Houve gargalhadas. Rafa se sentiu o próprio Boca do Inferno.
Na aula de Literatura, a professora Celeste pediu para ouvir. Riu em dois versos, ficou séria em outros dois, e então fez uma pergunta que Rafa não esperava:
— De quem é a culpa pelo pão de queijo frio?
— Ué... da cantina.
— E quem é a cantina? — insistiu ela.
Rafa abriu a boca e não respondeu.
A professora foi até a lousa e desenhou um mapa simples: Salvador no século XVII, capital da colônia, cheia de engenhos, igrejas e navios.
— O nosso poeta satirizava uma cidade inteira — explicou. — Ele mirava os comerciantes que vinham de fora, compravam o açúcar barato e vendiam caro tudo o que chegava nos navios. Zombava das autoridades que enriqueciam no cargo, dos falsos fidalgos que inventavam linhagens nobres, dos religiosos que pregavam uma coisa e faziam outra. A sátira dele era uma lente sobre os vícios de uma sociedade.
— Então ele também atacava pessoas — disse Rafa, defendendo-se.
— Às vezes, sim, e por isso arrumou muitos inimigos. Mas o que fez dele um grande poeta não foi o insulto. Foi mostrar como a Bahia colonial funcionava: quem ganhava, quem perdia, quem fingia ser o que não era.
Lia levantou a mão.
— Professora, então a sátira tem um lado moral? Ela ri para corrigir?
— Muitas vezes, sim. A sátira exagera para revelar. Mas exagero sem alvo vira só deboche.
Rafa voltou para casa pensativo. Releu o poema e notou que todo o humor caía sobre uma figura só: o cantineiro, seu Arlindo, um senhor simpático que sempre guardava um salgado para quem chegava atrasado. No poema, ele era ganancioso, preguiçoso e mal-humorado. Nada daquilo era verdade.
Rafa mandou uma mensagem no grupo do trio: "Acho que fiz uma sátira contra a pessoa errada."
Tomás respondeu primeiro: "Quem decide o preço do lanche?"
Lia completou: "E quem compra o pão de queijo congelado?"
Rafa ficou olhando para a tela por um bom tempo. Pela primeira vez, a piada não parecia tão engraçada.

chapters.title: Capítulo 5: O preço da língua
chapters.synopsis: O poema de Rafa chega ao seu Arlindo, que fica magoado. Rafa pede desculpas e aprende sobre as consequências que o poeta sofreu.
chapters.text:
Na segunda-feira, Rafa chegou à cantina e encontrou uma folha impressa presa no balcão com fita adesiva. Era o poema dele. Alguém tinha imprimido e colado ali, talvez de brincadeira. Seu Arlindo não estava sorrindo. Entregou o troco sem dizer uma palavra e não guardou salgado para ninguém.
Rafa passou a manhã inteira com um nó no estômago. No intervalo, esperou a fila acabar e se aproximou do balcão.
— Seu Arlindo, fui eu que escrevi aquilo.
O cantineiro tirou os óculos e limpou as lentes no avental, devagar.
— Eu sei, menino. Tem o seu nome embaixo.
— Era para uma aula sobre sátira. Mas eu errei o alvo. O senhor não tem culpa do preço, nem do pão congelado.
Seu Arlindo ficou um tempo calado. Depois soltou um suspiro.
— O preço quem decide é a empresa que aluga a cantina. O pão vem da fábrica deles. Eu só esquento. Já reclamei muitas vezes, sabe? Ninguém escuta.
Rafa arrancou a folha do balcão e a dobrou até ficar do tamanho de uma moeda.
— Desculpa.
— Desculpado. Mas escreve direito da próxima vez — respondeu o cantineiro, e pela primeira vez no dia quase sorriu.
À tarde, Rafa contou tudo à professora Celeste. Ela ouviu com atenção e então contou uma parte da história que ainda não tinha mostrado à turma.
— O nosso poeta também pagou pelo que escreveu. As sátiras dele irritaram tanta gente poderosa em Salvador que ele acabou degredado para Angola, do outro lado do Atlântico. Anos depois, pôde voltar ao Brasil, mas não à Bahia. Morreu em Recife.
— Por causa de poemas? — perguntou Rafa.
— Por causa de poemas que diziam o que muitos não queriam ouvir. A palavra tem força, Rafa. Por isso a sátira exige responsabilidade: saber quem você está criticando e por quê.
Rafa pensou no seu Arlindo limpando os óculos no avental.
— Professora, dá para fazer sátira sem machucar quem não merece?
— Dá. Os melhores satíricos miram quem tem poder, não quem está do lado de baixo do balcão. Eles riem de um sistema, de uma hipocrisia, de um vício coletivo.
Naquela noite, Rafa não escreveu nada. Ficou só pensando. Na mensagem do grupo, contou o que tinha acontecido. Lia mandou um coração. Tomás mandou uma frase: "Até o Boca do Inferno teve que atravessar o oceano. Você só teve que atravessar a cantina."
Rafa riu, pela primeira vez desde de manhã. E começou a imaginar uma nova sátira, desta vez com o alvo certo.

chapters.title: Capítulo 6: A cidade que vende tudo
chapters.synopsis: Rafa reescreve a sátira mirando o sistema, como o poeta fazia com a Bahia colonial. O trio descobre que as três vertentes se encontram.
chapters.text:
Durante uma semana, Rafa fez algo que nunca tinha feito: pesquisou antes de rimar. Leu na apostila sobre a Salvador do século XVII, a cidade onde o açúcar dos engenhos saía em navios rumo à Europa e de onde voltavam tecidos, vinhos e objetos de luxo vendidos a preços altos. Descobriu que o poeta comparava a cidade de antes, mais simples, com a cidade rica e ao mesmo tempo empobrecida do seu tempo. A riqueza passava pela Bahia, mas ia embora com os navios.
— É como se a cidade fosse um porto de passagem do próprio dinheiro — disse Rafa no intervalo.
— E a escola? — perguntou Lia.
Rafa sorriu. Tinha a resposta pronta.
— A escola é um pequeno porto também. Tudo é terceirizado, tudo vem de fora, tudo tem um preço. A cantina, a máquina de lanches, o uniforme, as excursões. Quem decide nunca aparece. Quem atende leva a culpa.
O novo poema não tinha nenhum nome. O eu lírico era um aluno que conversava com a própria escola, como o poeta conversava com a Bahia. No começo, lembrava a escola de antigamente, com o pátio de terra e a pipoca da festa junina. Depois, mostrava a escola de agora, brilhante e cara, onde até o ar-condicionado parecia ter etiqueta. O refrão perguntava, em tom de falsa inocência, quem lucrava com o pão de queijo frio.
Tomás leu e apontou um verso.
— Aqui você usou antítese: "tão rica de vitrines, tão pobre de recreio".
— E aqui tem um raciocínio que vira do avesso — completou Lia. — Isso é conceptismo, igual ao meu amigo advogado religioso aqui.
Tomás fez uma reverência.
Foi nesse momento que Lia abriu o caderno no triângulo que tinha desenhado no primeiro dia. Ligou as três pontas com a caneta roxa.
— Olha só. No meu poema, a beleza passa e eu sofro com isso. No do Tomás, o pecador sofre, mas tenta ganhar o perdão com a razão. No do Rafa, a cidade parece rica, mas está vazia por dentro. Em todos, tem uma coisa que parece uma e é outra.
— Aparência e essência — disse Tomás, lembrando da apostila.
— Contraste — completou Rafa. — O poeta não era três pessoas. Era uma pessoa olhando o mundo dividido de três jeitos.
Os três ficaram em silêncio, satisfeitos e um pouco surpresos com eles mesmos.
No dia seguinte, Rafa levou o poema novo à cantina antes de entregá-lo à professora. Seu Arlindo leu tudo, devagar, mexendo os lábios. No final, ergueu os olhos.
— Esse aqui eu colava no balcão.
Rafa saiu da cantina mais leve do que entrou, com um pão de queijo, ainda frio, embrulhado num guardanapo.

chapters.title: Capítulo 7: Luz e sombra no pátio
chapters.synopsis: No sarau barroco, o trio apresenta os três poemas. A plateia percebe o contraste que une as vertentes, e a professora fecha o estudo com uma surpresa.
chapters.text:
O pátio estava decorado com velas elétricas, tecidos dourados e uma faixa pintada pelos alunos do primeiro ano: "Sarau Barroco — luz e sombra". As cadeiras de plástico estavam todas ocupadas. Na primeira fila, a avó Nair segurava um vaso com uma orquídea nova. Ao fundo, de avental, seu Arlindo assistia encostado na porta da cantina.
A professora Celeste abriu a noite explicando o desafio: três alunos, três vertentes, um único poeta como inspiração. Pediu à plateia que prestasse atenção no que se repetia entre os poemas.
Lia foi a primeira. A voz tremeu no primeiro verso e se firmou no segundo. Falou da rosa que amanhece e anoitece na mesma face, do tempo jardineiro, do convite triste para aproveitar o jardim. Quando terminou, a avó levantou a orquídea como se fosse um troféu.
Tomás subiu em seguida, com as mãos nos bolsos para disfarçar o nervosismo. Leu o soneto da ovelha perdida devagar, marcando bem a virada dos tercetos. Na última estrofe, quando o eu lírico lembrava ao pastor a alegria do reencontro, um silêncio curioso tomou conta do pátio. Depois vieram os aplausos.
Por último, Rafa. Antes de começar, ele disse uma frase que não estava no roteiro:
— Escrevi duas versões deste poema. A primeira mirava a pessoa errada. Esta mira o lugar certo.
E leu a sátira da escola que vende tudo. A plateia riu nas rimas, ficou séria nas antíteses e explodiu no refrão sobre o pão de queijo frio. Lá no fundo, seu Arlindo aplaudiu de pé.
Quando o trio voltou ao palco junto, a professora fez uma pergunta ao público:
— O que os três poemas têm em comum?
Uma menina do nono ano levantou a mão.
— Todos falam de uma coisa bonita que esconde outra coisa. A rosa esconde a noite, o pecador esconde a esperança, a escola rica esconde um recreio pobre.
— Exatamente — disse Celeste. — O Barroco é a arte do conflito. O nosso poeta foi lírico, religioso e satírico, mas sempre olhou o mundo como um lugar dividido entre a aparência e a essência, o prazer e a morte, o pecado e o perdão.
Então ela pegou a velha caixa de papelão do primeiro dia e a entregou aos três.
— Para vocês guardarem.
Dentro havia três papéis novos. Lia abriu o seu: "Lírica, religiosa e satírica: você também consegue escrever as três." Os de Tomás e Rafa diziam a mesma coisa.
— Isso é uma armadilha — disse Rafa.
— É um convite — respondeu a professora. — Como todo bom poema barroco, as duas coisas ao mesmo tempo.
O trio desceu do palco rindo. Na saída, seu Arlindo estendeu a Rafa um guardanapo. Dentro, um pão de queijo. Desta vez, quentinho.

books.subject: en_lit
books.title: The Unseen Hour
books.premise: Year 11 student Maya dreads her unseen poetry mock, but over one week, with her friend Dev and her teacher Ms Oduya, she learns to read, plan and write about a stranger of a poem in forty-five minutes.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Forty-Five Minutes
chapters.synopsis: Ms Oduya announces an unseen poetry mock, and Maya panics until she is given a simple plan for dividing the time.
chapters.text:
The announcement arrived on a grey Tuesday, written in green marker across the whiteboard: UNSEEN POETRY MOCK – 45 MINUTES – NEXT FRIDAY.
Maya Lindqvist read it twice and felt her stomach drop. She liked poems when she had a week to think about them. She did not like the idea of meeting a stranger on paper and having to explain it before the clock ran out.
"You look like someone has cancelled the summer," said Dev Aranha, sliding into the seat beside her.
"I can't write about a poem I've never seen in forty-five minutes. I'll spend forty of them just reading it."
Ms Oduya must have heard, because she tapped the board with the cap of her pen. "That," she said to the whole class, "is exactly the problem we are going to solve. Nobody writes well when they are drowning. So we are going to build a raft."
She drew a long rectangle and cut it into four pieces. "Five minutes reading. Five minutes planning. Thirty minutes writing. Five minutes checking. The raft does not change, whatever the poem is."
Then she handed out a short poem, printed in the middle of a white page:

The kettle clears its throat at six,
a small grey engine on the hob.
My father stands in yesterday's shirt
and listens to it start to sob.
By seven it has learned to sing.
By eight the house has learned to speak.

"Read it once for the feeling," said Ms Oduya. "No pen. Then read it again with the pen and mark anything that surprises you."
Maya read it without the pen and felt something quiet and slightly sad. On the second reading she circled "sob" and "yesterday's shirt" and wrote tired? in the margin. She underlined the last two lines, where the sad sound turned into singing and the house began to speak.
"Now," said Ms Oduya, "tell me in one sentence what changes in this poem."
Dev put his hand up. "It goes from silent and sad to noisy and happy."
"Good. Can you make it sharper?"
Maya surprised herself by speaking. "The kettle's sound moves from sobbing to singing, so the morning moves from loneliness to family life."
Ms Oduya wrote it on the board. "That is a thesis. It is an argument, not a description. Everything you write in the thirty minutes should help to prove a sentence like that."
At the end of the lesson Maya copied the four-part rectangle into the back of her notebook. Under it she wrote: The poem is a stranger. The plan is not.
On the bus home she still felt nervous about Friday, but it was a smaller, tidier kind of nervous, the kind that fits inside a box.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Gate That Would Not Close
chapters.synopsis: Practising at home, Maya discovers how much a second reading can reveal, especially a shift in tone near the end of a poem.
chapters.text:
On Saturday morning Maya set a timer on her phone for five minutes and placed a new practice poem face down on the kitchen table. Her younger brother Felix watched from the doorway with a bowl of cereal.
"Are you defusing a bomb?" he asked.
"Sort of. Don't talk to me for five minutes."
She turned the page over.

My grandmother's gate would never close.
It leaned like someone half asleep,
its hinges orange, its paint in flakes,
a promise it forgot to keep.
We tied it shut with garden string.
She laughed and cut the string each spring.
Now the house belongs to strangers
and the gate is shut. It's new. It's straight.
I miss the way it used to wait.

On the first reading Maya simply let the poem happen. It felt gentle and funny at the start, then quiet and heavy at the end. She noticed she was holding her breath on the last line.
On the second reading she picked up her pencil. Next to "leaned like someone half asleep" she wrote simile – gate is like a person, lazy, comfortable. She circled "orange" and "flakes" and wrote old, rusty, but warm colour? She drew a star beside the grandmother cutting the string each spring. Why would she want the gate open?
Then came the line "Now the house belongs to strangers." Maya drew a thick line across the page just above it. Shift, she wrote. Past → present. Grandmother gone?
The poem did not say that the grandmother had died or moved away, and Ms Oduya had warned them about inventing facts. So Maya wrote carefully: the speaker has lost the house and perhaps the grandmother.
The timer buzzed. Felix, who had been silent with great effort, finally spoke. "So what's it about? A broken gate?"
"No," said Maya, and was surprised by how sure she sounded. "It's about how the gate being broken was actually the good part. The open gate meant you were always welcome. The new gate is perfect, but it's shut."
Felix chewed thoughtfully. "That's kind of sad."
"It is. But look at the short sentences here: 'It's new. It's straight.' They sound flat and cold, like the speaker doesn't care about the new gate at all."
She wrote her thesis at the bottom of the page: The poem turns a broken gate into a symbol of welcome, so its final neatness feels like a loss rather than a repair.
In the lesson on Monday, Ms Oduya read Maya's thesis aloud without saying whose it was. "Notice," she said, "that this writer did not just say what the poem is about. They spotted the turning point and built the argument around it. Most poems turn somewhere. Your second reading is where you find the hinge."
Dev leaned over and whispered, "Hinge. Gate. She's doing a pun."
Maya grinned and wrote the word hinge in her notebook, underlined twice.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Saying Something Worth Proving
chapters.synopsis: Dev's vague opening paragraph becomes a lesson in writing a clear, arguable thesis about a poem set in a harbour.
chapters.text:
Dev's opening paragraph was enormous. It filled almost half a page and said, in many different ways, that the poem was about a harbour and used a lot of interesting techniques.
"It's good, right?" he asked, pushing it towards Maya during the Wednesday practice. "I mention imagery, metaphor and personification. That's three techniques already."
Maya read the poem again before answering.

At dusk the boats come home like cattle,
nudging the harbour wall.
Their engines cough. Their ropes go slack.
The gulls complain to no one at all.
Only one mooring stays empty,
a gap the water will not fill.
The tide comes in. The tide goes out.
The harbour waits. The harbour's still.

"It's not bad," she said slowly. "But what are you actually arguing? Anyone could say the poem uses imagery. It's like saying a football match uses a ball."
Dev frowned. "So what should I say?"
"What's the most important thing in it? For me it's the empty mooring. Everything else is busy and noisy, the boats nudging, the engines coughing, the gulls complaining. Then there's one gap that nothing fills."
"A boat that didn't come back," Dev said quietly.
"Maybe. The poem doesn't say why. But the whole ending is about waiting."
Ms Oduya had stopped beside their desks. "Go on," she said.
Maya tried it out loud. "The poet contrasts the noisy, homely return of the boats with a single empty mooring, so the ordinary evening becomes a quiet image of loss and waiting."
"Better," said Ms Oduya. "Now, Dev, test it. Could someone disagree with that sentence?"
Dev thought. "Someone could say it's just a peaceful poem about evening."
"Exactly. A good thesis is a sentence that a sensible person could argue against. If nobody could disagree, you haven't said anything yet."
She went to the board and wrote three questions:
What happens in the poem?
What changes?
Why does that change matter?
"Your thesis answers the third question. And notice something about Maya's version: it mentions the contrast, which is a technique, but the technique serves the idea. Never list techniques for their own sake. Techniques are tools. Your thesis is what you are building."
Dev crossed out most of his paragraph. In its place he wrote two sentences. The first named the poem's setting and mood. The second said that the repeated, simple sentences at the end, "The tide comes in. The tide goes out.", made time feel endless for someone who was waiting.
"That's actually really good," Maya admitted.
"I know," said Dev. "I'm a genius who just needed a smaller paragraph."
Ms Oduya smiled. "Short openings are not lazy. In forty-five minutes, an introduction should take you two or three minutes, not ten. Say what you think, and then spend the rest of your time proving it."
Maya added a new line to the back of her notebook, under the rectangle and the word hinge: Thesis = an answer someone could argue with.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Climbing Paragraphs
chapters.synopsis: Using a poem about a night bus, Maya learns to build paragraphs that embed short quotations and climb from evidence to deeper analysis.
chapters.text:
By Thursday Maya could write a decent thesis in three minutes. The trouble now was what came after it. Her paragraphs started well and then stopped, like a staircase that ended in the middle of the air.
Ms Oduya looked at one of them and nodded. "You make a point, you quote, and then you say the quotation shows the point. That's two steps. Good paragraphs climb further."
She handed out the day's poem:

The night bus hums its single note
through streets that have forgotten noon.
A nurse, a baker and a boy
sit separate in its yellow room.
Nobody speaks. The windows hold
three faces floating on the dark,
and every stop the doors exhale
as if the bus were tired of work.

"Let's climb one paragraph together," said Ms Oduya. "Step one: the point. What is one thing the poem does?"
"It shows people being lonely even though they're together," said a girl near the window.
"Step two: the evidence. But keep it short. Embed it inside your own sentence."
Maya offered, "The passengers 'sit separate' in the bus."
"Good, two words, smoothly placed. Step three: zoom in. What about those two words?"
Maya looked again. "They both start with the same sound. S, s. It's quiet, like a hiss, like the hum of the bus."
"Sibilance," said Ms Oduya, writing it on the board. "Step four: widen out. How does that tiny detail connect to the whole poem?"
This was the part Maya always skipped. She thought for a moment. "The quiet sound matches how nobody talks. And later the windows 'hold three faces floating on the dark', so the people only meet as reflections, not in real life."
"And step five?"
"Link back to the thesis."
"Exactly." Ms Oduya drew a staircase with five steps: Point, Evidence, Zoom, Widen, Link. "In thirty minutes you will probably write three or four of these. Three good climbing paragraphs beat six short ones that stop halfway."
Dev raised his hand. "What about the last two lines? 'The doors exhale as if the bus were tired of work.' The bus is the only one that's alive. That's personification."
"Then why does it matter?" Ms Oduya asked.
Dev frowned, then brightened. "Because the bus is tired like the nurse and the baker. It's like another worker. The only thing in the poem that shares their feelings is a machine."
There was a short silence in the room, the kind that happens when an idea lands.
"That," said Ms Oduya, "is a paragraph climbing all the way to the top."
For homework Maya wrote one complete paragraph on the poem, counting her steps on her fingers. It took her eight minutes. She wrote a note to herself in the margin: Too slow. But every step is there.
At the bottom of the page Ms Oduya later added, in green ink: Speed comes with practice. Depth is harder to learn, and you have it.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Where the Lines Break
chapters.synopsis: A poem about snowmelt teaches Maya that form and structure, such as enjambment and stanza shape, can carry meaning too.
chapters.text:
"Today," said Ms Oduya, "we're going to talk about the part of the poem most of you ignore: its shape."
A few people groaned. Dev whispered, "Here comes the boring bit."
The poem on the sheet was arranged in short groups of two lines:

All winter the hill held its breath,
white and certain, keeping still.

Then March arrived and something
broke, a trickle, then a

rush of water down the
stones, the hill unlocking

its long, cold, clenched
fist into a field.

"Look before you read," said Ms Oduya. "What do you notice?"
"It's in pairs of lines," said someone.
"Couplets, yes. Now read it aloud, and pause only where there's punctuation."
Maya tried. The first stanza was calm and complete; each line ended where a thought ended. But from the second stanza onwards the sentences tumbled over the line breaks. "Something / broke" was split in half. "Then a / rush" made her almost fall into the next stanza.
"It feels like the words are running," she said. "Like the water."
"That's enjambment," said Ms Oduya, writing it on the board. "When a sentence runs on past the end of a line without a pause. And look where the poet breaks the line: right after 'something', so 'broke' lands at the start of the next line with a bump. The form does what the meaning describes."
Dev was frowning at the page, but not in a bored way anymore. "And the first stanza is the only one with full stops at the end of the lines. That's when the hill is frozen. So the frozen bit has frozen lines, and the melting bit has melting lines."
"Write that down before you forget it," said Ms Oduya. "That is exactly the kind of sentence examiners hope for."
She pointed to the last stanza. "What about 'long, cold, clenched'? Three adjectives, each with a comma."
"The commas slow you down," Maya said. "Like the hill is holding on until the very end. And then 'fist into a field' – the fist opens. The hand becomes land."
"A metaphor that turns into another image," said Ms Oduya. "And the alliteration on 'f' softens the ending."
Then she gave them a warning. "Form is not a box to tick. Never write 'The poem uses enjambment' and stop. Ask: why here? What does it do to the reader? If you can't answer that, leave it out. One idea about structure that is linked to meaning is worth more than five labels."
In her notebook Maya drew a quick picture: a block of ice on one side, a stream on the other. Under the ice she wrote end-stopped lines = control. Under the stream she wrote enjambment = release.
Dev looked at her drawing. "You should put that on a poster."
"Maybe after Friday," said Maya. She realised she was almost looking forward to it, which was the strangest feeling of the whole week.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: The Missing Ten Minutes
chapters.synopsis: In a full timed practice, Maya runs out of time and learns how to prioritise and finish with a strong conclusion.
chapters.text:
On Thursday afternoon, the day before the mock, Ms Oduya ran a full practice under exam conditions. Silence, clock on the wall, forty-five minutes.
The poem was about a lost glove:

One glove on the railing by the park,
a small wool hand that someone dropped,
held up by a stranger, waving
at a world that hasn't stopped.
Its other half is warm somewhere,
deep in a pocket, miles away.
It doesn't know it's incomplete.
It waits for winter every day.

Maya did her five minutes of reading perfectly. She found the hinge at "Its other half is warm somewhere", where the poem moved from what we see to what we imagine. Her thesis came quickly: The poem uses a lost glove to explore how separation can be invisible to the one who is left whole.
Then she began her first paragraph, on the image of the "small wool hand", and it went so well that she kept going. She zoomed in on "waving", widened out to the idea of being ignored, and then thought of another point, and another. When she finally looked up at the clock, she had used twenty-five minutes on a single paragraph.
Her heart thumped. Ten minutes left. She wrote a second paragraph quickly, but it was thin, only point and evidence. There was no time for a conclusion. When Ms Oduya said "Pens down," Maya's last sentence ended in the middle.
After the practice, she stayed behind, feeling the hot shame of having known the plan and not followed it.
"Your first paragraph is excellent," said Ms Oduya, reading it. "Probably the best thing you've written all term."
"But the rest is a disaster."
"The rest is a lesson. You didn't run out of ideas, you ran out of time. That is a much easier problem to fix." She took a sticky note and drew three small boxes. "Before you start writing, choose your three best points and put them in order. Give each one about eight or nine minutes. When the time for a box is up, finish your sentence, link back, and move on, even if you still have something to say."
"What if the best idea comes last?"
"Then put it first next time. Strongest idea, strongest paragraph. If the clock beats you, it beats your weakest point, not your best one."
Maya nodded slowly. "And the conclusion?"
"Two or three sentences. Don't repeat everything. Go back to your thesis and say one thing you understand now that you didn't at the start. With this poem, maybe that the glove is a picture of anyone who has been left behind without the other person noticing."
That evening Maya practised with a timer, writing only the plan and the first sentence of each paragraph. She did it for three different poems. Each time she put her strongest point first.
Felix watched her finish. "You look less scared than last week."
"I am," she said. "I made the worst mistake already. Better today than tomorrow."
Before bed she wrote in her notebook: Three boxes. Best first. Leave space for the ending.

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Tide Tables
chapters.synopsis: On the day of the mock, Maya meets a completely new poem and uses everything she has practised to write a calm, complete answer.
chapters.text:
Friday morning was bright and windy. The hall smelled of floor polish and nervous pencils. Maya sat at desk 14, three rows behind Dev, and looked at the clock: 9:00 exactly.
"You may begin," said the invigilator.
She turned the paper over.

My mother reads the tide tables
the way some people read the stars:
high water, low water, numbers
that tell her where the danger is.
She taught me which rocks drown first,
which paths the sea forgets to take.
Now I live inland, by a road
that never rises, never breaks,
and still I check the times each day
as if the sea might come my way.

First reading, no pen. Maya let the poem wash over her. It felt tender at first, then a little lonely, then oddly comforting.
Second reading, pen. She circled "the way some people read the stars" – a simile comparing practical numbers to something magical. She underlined "which rocks drown first" and wrote personification, danger, mother protecting. Then she drew her thick line above "Now I live inland". The hinge.
At 9:05 she started planning. She drew three boxes.
Box one, her strongest idea: the tide tables are a symbol of the mother's care, a kind of love written in numbers.
Box two: the contrast between the changing sea and the flat inland road that "never rises, never breaks".
Box three: the final rhyming couplet, "day" and "way", which closes the poem like a habit that cannot be broken.
Her thesis took two minutes: The speaker's daily habit of checking tide tables, even far from the sea, shows how a parent's protective love continues long after the danger has gone.
At 9:12 she began to write. She climbed each paragraph step by step: point, evidence, zoom, widen, link. When she noticed she was spending too long on the stars simile, she finished her sentence, linked back and moved on, even though she had more to say.
At 9:39 she wrote her conclusion. She said that the poem's final rhyme felt safe and settled, like a mother's voice, and that the speaker's habit was really a way of keeping the mother close.
At 9:40 she began checking. She fixed two spelling mistakes and added one missing quotation mark. At 9:45 the invigilator said, "Pens down."
Maya put her pen down. Her answer had a beginning, three full paragraphs and an end. It was not perfect. But it was complete.
Outside, Dev was waiting by the vending machine. "Box one, box two, box three?" he asked.
"Box one, box two, box three," she said. "You?"
"I finished with two minutes to spare. I didn't know what to do with them. I just read the poem again and enjoyed it."
Maya laughed. That was the strangest part of all: somewhere between the reading and the writing, she had started to enjoy it too.
The next Monday, Ms Oduya handed back the papers. Next to Maya's conclusion she had written in green ink: You met a stranger and listened carefully. That is what reading a poem is.
Maya took out her notebook and added one last line under all the others: The poem is a stranger. Now I know how to say hello.
